en: The Rāmapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad, the Rāmatāpinī Upaniṣad.
Om! O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.
May we praise you with steady limbs and bodies; may we attain that lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his uninjured wheel grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
The First Upaniṣad.
Om. When Hari, who is composed of consciousness, was born as Daśaratha within this Great Viṣṇu, he shone while remaining on earth, bestowing everything upon the lineage of Raghu. (1)
He was proclaimed as "Rāma" by the wise in the worlds;
by him the Rākṣasas met their death, either through his own prowess or otherwise. || 2 ||
Or again, it is called "Rāmanāma" (the Name of Rāma) on earth because he was delightful;
for, in the form of a mortal, he [overcame] the Rākṣasas just as Rāhu [overcomes] the mind-born god (Kāma). || 3 ||
Having thus deprived those kings worthy of sovereignty of their splendor,
he [established] the path of dharma through his conduct and the path of knowledge by name alone.
Likewise, through meditation, he attains dispassion and sovereignty by worshipping his own self;
thus, in accordance with reality, he shall truly be known as Rāma on this earth. (5)
"Yogis delight in the infinite, eternal bliss of the conscious Self;
thus, by the word 'Rāma,' this Supreme Brahman is designated. (6)
The conceptualization of forms for Brahman— which is composed of consciousness, non-dual, partless, and bodiless— is for the sake of the practical needs of its worshippers.
Regarding the deities of the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is the conceptualization of male and female limbs,
weapons, and so forth, numbering twenty-two, twenty-four, thirty-six, and thirty-two, as well as ten, twelve, and sixteen.
These eighteen hands, beginning with the conch and ending with the discus, have been described; likewise, their colors and the arrangement of their mounts are explained.
Thus, the conceptualization of Śakti and the army occurs in five ways within Brahman alone;
for that conceptualized body, there is the further conceptualization of the army and so forth. (10)

This mantra, which designates Brahmā and the other deities and possesses names such as "anvartha" (significant), must be recited by the practitioner; for without it, the Lord does not become propitious.
Now, the mantra expresses the meaning of the ritual action, the object, the sacrifice, and the agent;
because it both contemplates and protects, the mantra is the designator of everything that can be designated. (12)
This is the physical form of this fearless deity, which consists of the construction of a yantra;
for if worship is performed without the yantra, the deity does not become pleased. (13)
Thus ends the first Upaniṣad in the Rāmapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad. || 1 ||
The Second Upaniṣad
Svarbhū, consisting of light and possessing infinite forms, shines by his own power;
he to whom [the world] is equal in its states of living, creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
By means of the causal power of consciousness and through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas,
[the world arises], just as the great natural tree exists within the seed of a banyan.
In the very same way, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable *rāma* (ram);
and the forms [of the deities] are mounted upon the letter *repha* (r), as are the three powers (*śaktis*). Thus it is said. (3)
Thus ends the second Upaniṣad in the Rāmatāpinī Upaniṣad. || 2 ||
The Third Upaniṣad

Sītā and Rāma, who are identical with that [Brahman], are to be worshipped here; from them the fourteen worlds were born, by them they are sustained, and by them they are sent forth; thereafter, the human Rāma established them through his power of illusion (māyā).
"Salutation be to this one whose self is the life-breath of the world; one should first declare 'salutation' as being identical with the preceding quality. (2)
Thus ends the third Upaniṣad of the Rāmapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad. || 3 ||
The Fourth Upaniṣad
The word *namaḥ* denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), and it is sung as "one who delights in the Self" (*ātmārāma*). That which is its fourth case-ending is likewise sung as *māyā*. (1)

This mantra is the designator (vācaka) of Rāma, and Rāma is the designated (vācya); there is no doubt that for all practitioners, this is the union (yoga) of these two in terms of their fruit. || 2 ||
Just as one who is present before a person is made manifest by that person's name,
so too the mantra, which consists of seed-syllables, becomes manifest to the practitioner.
One should place the seed-power (bīja-śakti) on the right and left breasts;
the wedge (kīla) is to be meditated upon in the middle, according to one's own desired application.
This is the common procedure for all mantras;
herein Rāma, who possesses infinite forms, is equal to fire in his splendor.
If the universe consists of both the sentient and the insentient, then the world is composed of Agni and Soma;
it shines with Sītā as the moon shines with its radiance once it has arisen.
Naturally dark-complexioned, wearing yellow garments and matted locks, he has two arms, wears earrings and a jewel garland; steadfast, he holds a bow.
The Conqueror has a serene countenance and is adorned with eight bracelets;
by his very nature, he bears the mark of the Supreme Sovereign, the Source of the World.
The son of the princess of Kosala is embraced by Hemābhayā, who has two arms, is adorned with all ornaments, and holds a lotus; he is robust and radiant.
Then, on the right side, with Lakṣmaṇa holding a bow in his hand,
and likewise with the younger brother who has the luster of gold, there shall be three corners.
In that very same way, for that mantra whose subtle essence (*aṇu*) is within its own limbs, there arises thus the form of a triangle; into that the gods arrived.
And they offered praise to the Lord of the World, who was seated upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru): "Obeisance to Rāma, who can assume any form at will, and who consists of Māyā."
Salutations again and again to Oṃkāra, who is the form of the beginning of the Vedas;
salutations to Rāma, the consort of Ramā, the Śrīrāma who is the embodiment of the Self.

To the one who is the ornament of Jānakī’s body, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the one of auspicious limbs, the blessed hero of the Raghus, who has the form of the destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa. || 14 ||
O Rāmabhadra, O wielder of the great bow, O hero of the Raghus, O best of kings! O destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, grant us protection and prosperity. (15)
"Grant us sovereignty now, and likewise bring about the destruction of our enemies"—
having praised him thus, the gods and others remained happily with him.
For at that time, the sages praised the Asura Rāvaṇa in this way,
who had seized the wife of Rāma while she dwelt in the forest for his own sake.
He is known as Rāvaṇa, or he is called Rāvaṇa because of his roar;
under that pretext, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa themselves came to see Sītā.
Then, having seen the goddess and the asura on the ground, they dwelt there;
and having slain Kabandha, they went with his permission to Śabarī.
Honored by the son of the Wind, who was devoted to him, the lord of monkeys summoned Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa and related everything from beginning to end.
But he, being suspicious of Rāma and for the sake of proving the truth of Dundubhi's words, showed him his physical form; and Rāma hurled that very form at him.
Then Rāghava, having swiftly shattered the seven *sāla* trees, rejoiced;
delighted by that feat, the lord of monkeys, along with Rāma, went to his city.
Then Vālin’s younger brother, roaring, rushed from his house with great speed;
at that moment, Vālin emerged, and [the two] then [encountered] each other in battle.
Then, having slain him, Rāghava established Sugrīva on the throne;
thereafter, Sugrīva summoned the monkeys and said to those who know the directions: "Now [is the time]."
"Taking Maithilī today, give her [to Rāma] and go quickly!
Then Hanumān crossed the ocean and arrived at Laṅkā. || 25 ||
Having seen Sītā, slain the asuras, and likewise burnt the city himself,
he returned with Rāma and reported everything exactly as it had happened.
Then Rāma, assuming a form of wrath, summoned those monkeys;
taking his weapons along with them, he arrived at the city of Laṅkā. || 27 ||
Seeing her, he engaged in battle with the Lord of the Ocean,
who was joined in that combat by Ghaṭotkaca, Karṇa, and the conqueror of the Thousand-eyed Indra.
Having slain Bibhīṣaṇa there and established the daughter of Janaka [on the throne], he took her,
holding her on his lap, and departed for his own city with them.
Then the joy of the Raghus, seated upon the throne, was two-armed, holding a bow, serene in soul, and adorned with all ornaments.
Holding in his right hand the mudrā consisting of gnosis and in his left the one that radiates splendor,
the Supreme Lord, who is composed of consciousness, remains intent upon exposition.
Then, to his north and south, he should place Śatrughna and Bharata;
and Hanumān, the listener, should be in front, positioned at the apex of a triangle.
Below Bharata is Sugrīva, below Śatrughna is Vibhīṣaṇa;
to his west is Lakṣmaṇa, holding an umbrella and a chowrie.
Below that, those two hands should hold palm-leaf fans; furthermore, it should be triangular.
Thus, at the beginning, this [mandala] is joined with its own long limbs and the six corners.
The second [is worshipped] with Vāsudeva and the others in the southeast and other directions;
the third [is] Vāyusūnu (Hanumān), as well as Sugrīva and Bharata.
Then Dhṛṣṭi and Jayantaka were joined by Bibhīṣaṇa, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada—the crusher of enemies—and Jāmbavān. || 36 ||
Surrounded by Vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Aśoka, Dharmapāla, and Sumantra—these were his attendants. (37)
Then he was surrounded by these ten: the thousand-eyed Indra, Agni, Varuṇa who knows dharma, Anila (Vāyu), Indu (Candra), Īśa (Śiva), Dhātṛ, and Ananta. || 38 ||
Outside, he is to be worshipped with weapons, adorned by Nīla and others, and attended by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva. || 39 ||
Thus has it been declared by way of summary; now follows its detailed exposition:
having drawn a container of three lines, one should write two *tāra*s (oṃ-kāras) in the center.
Having written the seed-syllable (bīja) in the middle of that, one should write the object to be accomplished (sādhya) below it;
[the name of] the object should end in the accusative case, and likewise, the practitioner (sādhaka) above it should end in the genitive case.
One should write two *kuru*s at its sides and the syllable *ramā* within the seed-syllables; then the pure-minded practitioner should encircle all of that with two *praṇavas*.

In a six-cornered [diagram] possessing long [vowels], one should write the seed-syllables starting with the Heart-mantra; on the sides of the corners, one should write Ramā and Māyā, and at their tips, one should inscribe Anaṅga.
Having written the syllable KRODHA within the corners of the triangles, one should write the mantra around it;
then, one should draw three circles containing an eight-petaled lotus and inscribe the vowels upon that lotus.
Then one should write the eight groups of letters upon the filaments and the eight petals;
within those, one should inscribe the syllables of the *mālāmantra* in a number equal to the waves (seven).

Having thus written the five syllables at the beginning, one should again draw an eight-petaled lotus; having inscribed the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa upon its petals, one should place the syllable *ramā* in its filaments.
Outside of that, one should draw a twelve-petaled [lotus] with the twelve-syllable mantra:
"Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya. (47)
One should inscribe the letters from *ā* to *kṣa* in a circular form upon the filaments;
outside of that, having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus, one should place the heart-mantra on its filaments.

The practitioner of mantra should inscribe the twelve-syllable mantra, joined with armor (*varma*), weapon (*astra*), and bow (*dhanus*), upon the petals; he should likewise inscribe the mantras of Viriñci and the other deities at their joints.
One should correctly write *hraṃ*, *sraṃ*, *bhraṃ*, *vraṃ*, *lū*, *aṃ*, *śraṃ*, and *jraṃ* outside of that;
then, a great lotus with thirty-two petals, joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*.
One should carefully inscribe the syllables of the king of mantras upon those petals,
and one should indeed meditate there upon the eight Vasus and the eleven Rudras.
Outside of that, one should place the twelve Ādityas, Dhātṛ, and Vaṣaṭkāra;
then the earthly enclosure (bhūgṛha), enriched with thunderbolts and tridents, and provided with three lines.
And at the entrance, it should be adorned with heaps [of offerings] and so forth, joined by hooded serpents:
Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, and Padmaka.
Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and Gulika are proclaimed as the eight;
having thus drawn the mandala, [one should place them] in its cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should likewise draw the Nārasiṃha and Vārāha [mantras], as well as the two mantras;
the *kūṭa* [syllable] is joined with the letter *ra*, the *anugraha*, the moon, the *nāda*, the *śakti*, and so forth.
The one who is celebrated as Nṛsiṃha for the rite of slaying the planets [is the deity]; and the boar-seed mantra consists of the final syllable, the feet, the Lord, space, the bindu, and the nāda.

And here, the syllable *huṃ* is declared to be Rāma’s root mantra; it consists of the *tāra* (oṃ), the salutation (*namaḥ*), sleep (*nidrā*), remembrance (*smṛti*), and the *kāmikā* (the desire-granting seed-syllable).
Joined with Rudra, adorned with Vahni, Medhā, and Amara;
Dīrghā joined with Krūra, and then Hlādinī joined with Dīrgha. (58)
Kṣudhā, Krodhinī, Amoghā, and Viśvā, as well as Medhā, Dīrghajvālinī, Susūkṣmā, and Mṛtyurūpiṇī. (59)
It is accompanied by *pratiṣṭhā*, *hlādinī*, *tvak*, *kṣvela*, *prīti*, and *sāmarā*;
it is joined with *jyotis*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *agni*, and is conjoined with the white *anusvāra*.

The fifth root of the Kāmikā [is] the letter ending in *ta*, followed by the one ending in *tha*; then that same letter with *ā* and *ananta* (the nasal *m*), joined with the long vowel [ā], is Vāyu; joined with the subtle [vowel *u*], it is Viṣa.
Kāmikā joined with Kāma, then Rudra joined with Sthirātapa;
Tāpinī joined with Dīrgha, Bhū, Anala, Anantaga, and Anila. (62)

Time (kāla), whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, joined with the breath (prāṇa) and water (ambhas) along with knowledge (vidyā); likewise, the enemy of the yellow one (pītārāti) ending in the letter *la*, joined with the womb (yoni), followed by obeisance (nati). || 63 ||
One should write the name of that Rāma, consecrated in the kingdom, according to the stated sequence, including his own qualities ending with the forty-seven qualities of excellence. (64)
This all-encompassing yantra, previously described and practiced by the sages, grants liberation to its practitioners and increases their lifespan and health. (65)
It grants sons to those who are childless; indeed, what need is there for further elaboration?
For here, in an instant, they duly attain dharma and all other goals as well.
This supreme secret is difficult even for the Lord to traverse;
this yantra has been fully described, and it must not be given to an ordinary person.
Thus ends the fourth Upaniṣad of the Rāmapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad.
The Fifth Upaniṣad
Oṃ! Having purified the elements and performed the worship of the door, one should remain serene, seated upon a lotus or similar seat;
during the rite of worship, one should perform the adoration of the base, the top, and the sides of the pedestal, as well as the worship of the central lotus. || 1 ||
Having prepared a soft, smooth, and well-stuffed cushion and having worshipped the Teacher upon a jeweled throne,
one should visualize the power called the Support (Ādhāra), along with the Tortoise and the Serpent, beneath the earth-lotus at the base of one's own seat.

Having bowed to Vighneśa, Durgā, Kṣetrapāla, and Vāṇī, as well as the seed-syllables (bījas) and others located in the directions starting from the southeast (Agni), and likewise to Dharma and the other [Puruṣas] on the feet of the pedestal, one should worship the deities in the directions beginning with the east.
In the center, one should meditate in sequence on the splendors of the sun, moon, and fire, each successively worshipped by the preceding ones;
and one should likewise meditate in sequence upon the three circles of rajas, sattva, and tamas, enriched with their respective seed-syllables.

Then, one should worship the Self within the Āśā and Vyāśā [vāyus], or the Inner Self (antarātman), or the Supreme Self (paramātman) within; and the Knowledge-Self (jñānātman) in its directions, as well as Māyā and Vidya in the Kalā, Aparatattva, and Paratattva.
One should worship Vimalā and the other Śaktis, honor the Lord, and invoke Him;
[one should also worship] with the limbs (aṅga), the arrays (vyūha), the wind-born [deities], and others, as well as with the Guardians of the Quarters beginning with Dhṛti, and their weapons.

One should worship Rāghava with sandalwood and other offerings, as well as various principal and diverse honors, by means of sages such as Vasiṣṭha and leaders like Nīla; and having properly performed recitations and other rites for him.
I bow to Rāma, who is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; who is the support of such a world;
who bears the mace, discus, conch, and lotus; and who is the enemy of worldly existence—he who meditates upon him attains liberation. || 8 ||
Rāghava, who is all-pervading, then vanished while holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
accompanied by Ramā, his younger brother, his city, his followers, and all the worlds.
Those who are devoted to Him, having obtained their desires and enjoyed them, likewise go to the supreme state;
and those stainless ones who recite these verses, which grant all desired objects, attain liberation.
Thus ends the fifth Upanishad of the Rāmapūrvatāpiny-upaniṣad.
The Rāmottaratāpinī Upaniṣad
First Section.
The Worship of Avimukta.
Oṃ. Bṛhaspati said to Yājñavalkya:
"Kurukṣetra is the sacrificial ground of the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings. (1)
"Kurukṣetra is indeed unconditioned (Avimukta), the sacrificial ground of the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings.
Therefore, wherever one goes, one should think: 'This is indeed Kurukṣetra, the sacrificial ground of the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings.
For here, when the vital breaths of a living being depart, Rudra teaches the liberating Brahman (Tāraka-brahma), by which he becomes immortal and attains liberation."
Therefore, one should cultivate the state of non-liberation; one should not abandon the state of non-liberation. || 2 ||
"So it is, Yājñavalkya. || 3 ||
Thus ends the first section.
The Second Section.
Regarding the six-syllabled mantra of Rāma, its nature as a "savior" (tāraka) was then explained; Bhāradvāja questioned Yājñavalkya:
"What is the savior? What does it save? || 1 ||

Yājñavalkya said: "The Tāraka [mantra] consists of Dīrghānala preceded by Bindu, followed again by Dīrghānala, then Māyā, and 'Obeisance to Candra, obeisance to Bhadra'— these are of the nature of Brahman."
It should be worshipped as that which is called Truth-Consciousness-Bliss. || 2 ||
The letter *a* becomes the first syllable;
the letter *u* becomes the second syllable;
the letter *m* becomes the third syllable.
The fourth syllable is half a mora;
the dot (bindu) is the fifth syllable;
the resonance (nāda) is the sixth syllable.
Because it delivers one across [the ocean of transmigratory existence], it is the "Deliverer" (tāraka).
Know that very thing to be the Brahman that is the Deliverer;
it is to be understood as that which is to be meditated upon.
Because it delivers one from the great fear of the cycle of existence consisting of conception, birth, old age, and death, it is therefore called the six-syllabled Tāraka (the Savior). || 3 ||
The Fruit of the Recitation of the Tāraka:
The Brahmin who constantly studies this Tāraka Brahman crosses over evil; he crosses over death.

He overcomes the killing of a Brahmin; he overcomes the killing of an embryo; he overcomes the killing of a hero; he overcomes the killing of all beings; he overcomes cyclic existence; he overcomes everything.
He becomes one who relies upon the Unliberated;
he becomes great; and he attains immortality. || 4 ||
Regarding Rāma’s identity as the meaning of the *praṇava*, there are these verses here:
"The son of Sumitrā, the creator of the universe, was born from the syllable *A*."
Śatrughna, who is composed of the nature of fire, is born from the syllable *ukāra*.
Bharata, however, consists of wisdom and arises from the syllable *ma*;
Rāma consists of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) and is the singular embodiment of the bliss of Brahman. (6)
By virtue of the proximity of Śrī Rāma, she acts as the support of the universe and brings about the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all embodied beings.
She is to be known as Sītā, designated as the Root Nature (mūlaprakṛti);
because she is the syllable Om (praṇava), the exponents of Brahman call her Prakṛti. Thus [it is said].

The true nature of the Praṇava and its meaning: "Om"—this syllable is all this; its further explanation is that whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever will be—all that is indeed the syllable Om.
And whatever else transcends the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Om.
For all this is Brahman. This Self is Brahman; this very Self has four quarters. || 9 ||
The first quarter is Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is the waking state, who is conscious of external objects, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences gross objects. || 10 ||
The second quarter is Taijasa, whose sphere is the dream state, who is conscious of internal objects, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences subtle objects. 11.
That state in which one who is asleep desires no object of desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever is deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
In the state of deep sleep, he has become unified; he is indeed a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*) consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
The third foot is the wise one (prājña), who experiences bliss and whose mouth is the mind (ceto-mukha). || 12 ||
He is the Lord of all, He is the All-knowing, He is the Inner Ruler; He is the source of all, for from Him come the origin and dissolution of all beings.

It is neither inwardly conscious, nor outwardly conscious, nor conscious of both; it is neither consciousness, nor unconsciousness, nor a mass of consciousness; it is invisible, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, inconceivable, and indescribable.

They consider the Fourth to be non-expressive, having the nature of self-realization as its essence, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual; that is the Self, that is to be known. 14.

I am indeed that which is the unification of the inner self and Brahman—eternally luminous, free from ignorance and its effects, the remover of the bondage of one's own self, forever devoid of duality, of the nature of bliss, the pure existence that is the substratum of all, and in whom the darkness and delusion of ignorance have been dispelled. Thus should I be contemplated. 15.
Oṃ tat sat! Rāmacandra, whose nature is consciousness, is the Supreme Brahman. I am He; Oṃ! I am Rāma, the end of all, the auspicious supreme light, the essence—Oṃ! || 16 ||
Thus, having taken up the self with the mind, one should unify it with Brahman. || 17 ||

"Liberation always comes from the knowledge of Rāma; those who declare in truth, 'I am Rāma,' are certainly not worldly beings, but are indeed Rāma himself—of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
"He who knows thus becomes liberated," so said Yājñavalkya. || 19 ||
Thus ends the second section.
The Third Section.

Then Atri asked Yājñavalkya about the true nature of that which is free from both the external and the internal: "How may I come to know that one who is infinite, unmanifest, perfectly full, blissful, and the singular conscious Self? || 1 ||
Yājñavalkya said: "That which is Avimukta is to be meditated upon;
this is the infinite, unmanifest Self, and it is established in Avimukta. || 2 ||
"On what is that 'unreleased' [state] established? || 3 ||
It is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī. || 4 ||
"What indeed is the Varaṇā, and what is the Nāsī? || 5 ||
Because it wards off all defects committed in other births, it is therefore called Varaṇā; because it destroys all evils committed by the senses, it is therefore called Nāsī. || 6 ||
And what is his abode? || 7 ||
The junction between the eyebrows and the nose is indeed the junction between this world and the world beyond;
the knowers of Brahman worship this junction as the *sandhyā*.
"He is to be meditated upon as the Unreleased. He who knows this thus declares the knowledge of the Unreleased. || 8 ||
The Instruction on the Śiva-provided Rāma-tāraka for those about to die:
Then the Bull-bannered Lord replied to him, "In Kāśī, I have recited the mantra of Śrī Rāma."
Even through thousands of Manvantaras, by means of recitation, fire-oblations, worship, and other such rites.
Then the blessed Śrī Rāma, being pleased, said to Śaṅkara: "O Supreme Lord, choose whatever you desire; I shall grant it to you. Thus [he spoke].
Then the Lord asked Śrī Rāma, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss:
"Furthermore, if an embodied being should die at Maṇikarṇikā, in my own sacred field, or on the banks of the Gaṅgā, there is no other boon superior to the liberation of that person. Thus [he spoke].
Then Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord of Gods, let even the worms, insects, and other such creatures who have died anywhere in this field of yours be swiftly liberated; let it not be otherwise. (12)
In your field of Avimukta, for the sake of the liberation of all,
I am ever present there within stone images and other such forms.
O Śiva, whoever worships me with devotion in this sacred field by means of this mantra, I shall liberate them from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; do not grieve.
Those who receive the six-syllabled mantra from you or even from Brahmā shall become perfected in the mantra while living; liberated, they attain me.
O Śiva, whoever you yourself shall personally instruct in my mantra— whether it be one who is about to die or anyone else— that person shall become liberated.
Thus it was spoken by the illustrious Rāmacandra.
The Fourth Section.
The mantras that bestow the direct vision of Rāma:
Now Bhāradvāja said this to Yājñavalkya,
"By which mantras, when praised, does Śrī Rāmacandra become pleased?"
"He reveals his own self to them; therefore, tell us, O Blessed One.
Yājñavalkya said:
"In the past, Brahmā was thus instructed by Śrī Rāmacandra in the world of truth (satyaloka); now, he pays homage with this very verse."
To Viṣṇu, the bearer of universal forms, Nārāyaṇa, the one free from ailment,
the singular consciousness of perfect bliss, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
Meditating upon Brahman with his mind, he praised the Supreme Lord:
"Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, the non-dual supreme bliss, the Self, that which is the Supreme Brahman—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations, salutations unto Him! (1)
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he who is the self of unbroken, singular essence—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 2 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; that which is the nectar of the bliss of Brahman, and that which is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 3 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, that Tāraka Brahman; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—salutations, salutations unto him! || 4 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he who is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; he who is the soul of all the gods; he who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 5 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he is all the Vedas with their limbs, their branches, and their Itihāsas and Purāṇas—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. 6.
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he who is the individual soul (jīvātman) is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 7 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, the inner self of all beings; to him, who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, be salutation after salutation. || 8 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; whatever states there are—gods, asuras, humans, and so forth—and the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 9 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he who is the incarnations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others—homage, homage to him, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ! || 10 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is Prāṇa—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 11 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord, whose self is the fourfold internal organ;
to Him who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, salutations again and again. || 12 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is Yama, and who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 13 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One;
he who is the Destroyer of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 14 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, and he who is Death—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation: Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! || 15 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; that which is the nectar of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 16 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; to him, and to the five great elements, and to Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 17 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord, the soul of all that is stationary and moving;
to him, who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, be salutation after salutation. || 18 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he is the five fires, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 19 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; those which are the seven great utterances—bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 20 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; that which is the Vidyā of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 21 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; she who is Sarasvatī is Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ. To him indeed, salutations again and again. || 22 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; she who is Lakṣmī is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. To Him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 23 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; she who is Gaurī is Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ. To him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 24 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; she who is Jānakī is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 25 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; and that which is the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 26 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he who is the Sun, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 27 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is Soma is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 28 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; and whatever constellations there are in the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again! || 29 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; and those who are the nine planets—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 30 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; and those who are the eight guardians of the world—homage, homage to him, to Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. || 31 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; and those who are the eight Vasus—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 32 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, as are the eleven Rudras;
to him, to Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, be salutation after salutation. || 33 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; and those who are the twelve Ādityas—to him, indeed, to that Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, be salutation after salutation. || 34 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; whatever has been, is, and will be—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 35 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; salutations again and again to Him who pervades the exterior of the universe—the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar. || 36 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is Hiraṇyagarbha, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 37 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; that which is primordial nature (prakṛti) is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 38 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is the syllable Oṃ, and who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 39 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he who consists of the four half-morae—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 40 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is the Supreme Person, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 41 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, and he who is Maheśvara—homage again and again to him, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ! || 42 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is Mahādeva—homage, homage to him, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ! || 43 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Vāsudeva, who is Mahāviṣṇu—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 44 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is the Supreme Self, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 45 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One; he who is the self of pure consciousness, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 46 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord; he whose self is the singular essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 47 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed One, the non-dual supreme bliss, the Self.
To him who is existence-consciousness-bliss, the non-dual absolute consciousness-Self, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. Thus.
Brahmā said to them: "Praise the God constantly with forty-seven mantras;
then the God will become pleased and reveal His own self. Therefore, whoever praises the God constantly with these mantras, he beholds the God."
"He goes to immortality"—thus ends the Mahopaniṣad.
Thus ends the fourth section.
The Fifth Section.
The Greatness of the Six-Syllabled Mantra of Rāma.
Then Bhāradvāja, having approached Yājñavalkya, said to him:
"Please declare the greatness of the King of Mantras, the Śrī Rāma mantra. || 1 ||
Yājñavalkya said:
He is self-luminous, the supreme light, consisting solely of consciousness through his own experience;
that very [reality] is remembered as the first syllable of the name "Rāmacandra," beginning with the letter *ma*. || 2 ||
The bliss of unbroken, singular flavor, denoting the Tāraka Brahman, is to be well understood as "Rāmāya," which consists of the nature of truth, bliss, and consciousness. || 3 ||
The word "namas" is easy to understand and is the singular embodiment of perfect bliss;
all gods who seek liberation always bow to it within their hearts. Thus [it is said].
Whoever constantly studies this king of mantras, the six-syllabled mantra of Śrī Rāmacandra, becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind;
he becomes purified by the sun; he becomes purified by the moon.
He becomes purified by Brahmā; he becomes purified by Viṣṇu; he becomes purified by Rudra; he becomes known by all the gods;
he has performed all sacrifices; by him [the recitation] of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Rudras...
When recited one hundred thousand times, the fruits [of the practice] are realized;
ten million times ten million recitations of the *praṇavas* are accomplished.
It purifies ten preceding generations and ten succeeding generations.
He becomes a purifier of the assembly; he becomes great;
and he attains immortality. || 5 ||
Verses demonstrating the majesty of the King of Mantras:
Here are these verses:
"He is the bestower of desired boons among the Gāṇapatyas, the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the Sauras."
Even among all Vaiṣṇava mantras, the Rāma-mantra yields the most abundant fruit.
Among the mantras of Gāṇapatya and others, this six-syllabled mantra is superior by millions upon millions of times; it bestows its fruit even without effort.
This six-syllabled mantra is the warder-off of the flood of all sins;
it is proclaimed as the King of Mantras, the most excellent of all. (8)
Whatever evil has been committed during the day, or that which arises from a fortnight, a month, a season, or a year—
it consumes it all without remainder, just as fire consumes a mountain of cotton.
Thousands of killings of Brahmins committed both knowingly and unknowingly, as well as tens of thousands of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and violations of the preceptor’s bed. || 10 ||
Even thousands of millions upon millions of sins arising from minor transgressions—all of them perish through the recitation of Rāma’s mantra. (11)
By the power of the Rāma-mantra, ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and others, as well as kūṣmāṇḍas and brahmarākṣasas, flee far away.
This mantra will accomplish worldly sovereignty, otherworldly rewards such as heaven, absolute liberation, and even the state of the Blessed Lord.
It shall swiftly destroy the sin of killing domestic or wild animals, whatever accumulated evil has been spoken, and whatever sin arises from the drinking of intoxicants.
O Rāma, everything arising from the consumption of forbidden food, produced by false knowledge, dissolves simply through the recitation of this mantra. 15.
Whatever sin has arisen from stealing the gold of a Vedic scholar,
as well as that from the theft of gems and other valuables— that too one should quickly destroy.
By killing a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, a man accumulates sin through delusion; whatever that may be, he should destroy it as well.
Even if one has, out of delusion, approached a mother or women who are forbidden, Rāma shall destroy even that [sin] by means of this mantra. 18.
Whatever has been accumulated through association with those most wicked in their great sins, one may destroy that by means of conversation, sharing a bed, a seat, or a meal. (19)
Whatever sin has arisen from the killing of a father or mother, and whatever [sin] was committed intentionally—all this is dissolved merely by the performance of this [rite]. || 20 ||
Even that sin which cannot be removed even by hundreds of expiatory rites prescribed for sacred sites such as Prayāga—this [practice] shall swiftly destroy it as well. (21)
Having intentionally committed a sin even in all the fields of merit, such as Kurukṣetra and others, one should personally cause that too to perish quickly.
Even that sin which cannot be removed by arduous penances such as the *taptaparāka* and various *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts,
it shall swiftly destroy.
Even by means of various kinds of gifts, such as gold equal to one's own weight, that [merit] would not diminish even slightly; yet he would cause even that to perish quickly. (24)
Thus, whatever sin has been committed intentionally during the three states [of waking, dreaming,
and deep sleep], it is dissolved without remainder by the mere recollection of the mantra.
Thus, in these three states, whatever fundamental bond and sin exists—
all of this perishes through the instruction of the mantra.
The defects of the seed of Brahmā and those arising from the transgression of observances, belonging to both women and men, have been destroyed by this mantra. (27)
In whichever regions Rāmabhadra is worshipped,
there shall never be any fear of famine or other such calamities.
Peaceful, with a serene countenance, free from anger, and affectionate toward his devotees—there is no mantra equal to this one to be found even in the worlds. (29)
When Rāma is properly propitiated, he indeed becomes pleased quickly;
he bestows longevity, sovereignty, and at the end, that which is the station of Viṣṇu.
This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
"In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛcs, in the highest heaven, wherein all the gods have settled;
he who does not know that—what will he do with the Ṛcs? But those who know it, they sit together here. (31)
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky.
The wise, ever-vigilant, and inspired poets kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Oṃ, "Truth," thus ends the Upaniṣad. || 34 ||
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain the lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his uninjured wheel-rims grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Rāmottaratāpinī Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the Rāmatāpinyupaniṣad.
